title: What do you say?
hookLine: "Zeno said this," but what do you say? Stop only quoting (Letters 33)

cards: Lucilius has been enjoying the short, sharp sayings Seneca tucks at the end of his letters, mostly lines from Epicurus. He asks for more. And in the thirty-third letter, Seneca says, in effect: no.
Not because the sayings are bad. Because Lucilius is old enough now to have his own. An odd thing to hear on a path that has quoted old teachers for over a year.
It's the moment a teacher gently takes away the training wheels.

teach.b: Epicurus' school, Seneca says, puts a few brilliant lines up front. The Stoic writers are different: the good is spread all through, so plucking out single flowers misses the field.
It's fine for a child to learn a few sayings by heart, he says. But for a grown man to lean only on a notebook of other people's lines is embarrassing. Then comes the jab that gives today its title.
Zeno said this. And you? Cleanthes said that.
And you? How long will you march under someone else's command? Seneca grumbles about those who never write anything of their own, but always hide in another's shadow, explaining.
Remembering, he says, isn't the same as knowing. Remembering is holding something someone gave you to keep. Knowing is making it yours.

The great teachers who went before, he says, are not our masters but our guides. The truth is open to everyone, and plenty of it is still left for those who come after. That's the posture this path hopes for.
Epictetus, Seneca, and soon Marcus all get a hearing. Sooner or later, though, the question turns around.
Not what did they say. What do you say?

how: Some readers of the Stoics keep a notebook where, after copying a teacher's line, they try to restate it in their own words and test it against their own life.

o: the Epicurean whose sayings close Seneca's letters
Seneca's own teacher, who taught him to write
the Stoic in Seneca's jab: he said this; and you?

games.q: your own voice — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca refuses more sayings because Epicurus's lines are bad
he says the time for living on a notebook of quotes has passed.
Seneca says the truth is open to everyone, with much left to find
those who went before are guides, not masters.
for Seneca, remembering a teaching is the same as knowing it
remembering holds what you were given; knowing makes it yours.

games.q: you're Lucilius, a grown man, and you ask Seneca for another batch of quotations. what does he send?
o: a challenge: Zeno said this, and you?
games.why: Seneca tells him to stop marching under someone else's command and start speaking for himself.

practice: Bring to mind one idea from these letters that has stuck with you, maybe the water clock, or start poor. Let go of Seneca's words and try it in your own plain words, as you'd say it to a friend over coffee, then once more, simpler.
When it feels like yours, hold it.

wordCard.voice: Zeno. Seneca's challenge: Zeno said this, Cleanthes said that, but the teachers are guides, not masters, and the next line is yours. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what do I say. The old teachers are guides, not masters. Until tomorrow.
